[Page 537]

Qur'an 104:1–4: "Woe to every backbiter and slanderer, who has gathered wealth and counted it. He thinks his wealth will make him immortal. No! [Surah al-Humazah 104:1–4]"

The phrase "Woe to him" (waylun lahu) is a supplication against the person referred to by the preposition *li*, that woe should befall him. *Wayl* means evil condition, as has been mentioned more than once before, including in the words of God Most High: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say, "This is from God"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:79], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The supplication here is used as a threat of punishment.

The word "every" (kull) indicates that those threatened by this warning are a group, namely those who made the mocking and slandering of Muslims their habit. These are the same people mentioned earlier in connection with the occasion of revelation of the surah.

*Humazah* and *lumazah* follow the pattern *fu'alah*, a form indicating frequent occurrence of the act derived from it, and that it has become a habit for its doer, like the expressions *duhakah* ("one who laughs much") and *lu'anah* ("one who curses much"). The origin of this is that the pattern *fu'al* (with a damma then a fatha) occurs for intensive emphasis of the active participle (*fa'il*), as al-Radi stated explicitly in his commentary on al-Kafiyah (*Sharh al-Kafiyah*): one says *rajulun huṭam* (a man who is harsh) if he has little mercy toward livestock, i.e., and animals.

From this come the expressions *khuta'* (with a Arabic *kha'* and a dotted letter, and a ta' with two dots above) which means the skilled guide in directing the way. When further intensification in the description is intended, the *ha'* is added to it, as it is added in *'allamah* and *rahhalah*. So they say: *rajulun huṭamah*, *duḥakah*, and from this *humazah*. By this second intensification it conveys that this trait has grown in him until it became a habit to which he has become accustomed, as in *al-Kashshaf*. They have also said that *'uyabah* is equivalent to *'ayyabah*. Among the patterns, some are heard with the description in both forms *fu'al* and *fu'alah*, such as *huṭam* and *huṭamah*, without a *ha'* and with a *ha'*. Among the patterns, some are heard only as *fu'alah* and not *fu'al*, like *rajul duḥakah*. Among them are some heard only as *fu'al* and not *fu'alah*, and that is in insult together with the vocative particle: *yā ghudar* ("O treacherous"), *yā fusaq* ("O wicked"), *yā khubuth* ("O vile"), *yā lukka'* ("O fool").

Al-Muradi said in his commentary on al-Tashil (*Sharh al-Tashil*): "Some of them said: it is not heard other than these and is not analogized upon." [Page 537 continues] And from Sibawayh it is reported that he permitted analogy upon them in the vocative. I say: On the view of Sibawayh, al-Hariri built his statement in the thirty-seventh *maqamah*: "Silence, O *'uqaq* (rebellious one), O you who are the choking and the throat-catching."

*Humazah* is a descriptive adjective derived from *al-hamz*, which is for one person to find fault with another by a gesture with the eye, or with the cheek, or with the head, in his presence or when he turns away. It is said: *hamiz* and *hammaz*. The form *fu'alah* indicates the firm establishment of the attribute in the one described.

*Humazah* occurs as a description of an omitted noun, whose estimated sense is: "woe to every person who is a *humazah*." When its described noun is omitted, the description stands in its place and is then annexed to *kull*.

*Lumazah* is a descriptive adjective derived from *al-lamz*, which is confronting someone with a fault. Its form indicates that this attribute is a habit (*malakah*) of its possessor, as in *humazah*.

These two attributes belong to the way the people of polytheism treated the believers on that day. Whoever among the Muslims treats a fellow member of his religion in a similar way has a share in this threat.

Whoever among the Muslims is characterized by any part of this blameworthy character toward the people of his own religion, it is a trait of the people of polytheism. It is a blameworthy trait that enters into harming a Muslim, and it has many degrees according to the strength of the harm and its repetition. Only striking a Muslim and reviling the Companions, may God be pleased with them, are counted among the major sins.

Persisting in this harm, by making it a habit, leads back to persisting in minor sins, which is itself counted among the major sins.

[Page 538] God followed ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾ to add further reproach to His two blameworthy descriptions by the attribute of greed for wealth. This arises only from the stinginess of the soul and fear of poverty. The purpose of this is to include those who were known for mocking and slandering Muslims, those who were said to be the cause of the surah's revelation, in this threat by specifying them.

The relative noun in ﴿who has gathered wealth﴾ is another attribute (*na't*). *Alladhi* was not joined with a *wa* (and), because mentioning several attributes for one described noun may occur without a conjunction, as in His words, Most High: ﴿Do not obey every oath-maker, contemptible, [Qalam 68:10] a slanderer, going about with gossip, [68:11] a hinderer of good, transgressing, sinful, [68:12] brutal and after that base-born. [68:13]﴾

Wealth (*al-mal*) refers to the gains of a person that benefit him and suffice for the expense of his needs of food, clothing, and what is obtained from them, such as livestock and fruit-bearing trees. The term *mal* among each group of the Arabs became dominant for what was most abundant among their possessions. Thus among the tent-dwellers the name *mal* came to predominate for camels. Zuhayr said:

*So I see them all in the morning, tying them, healthy camels of wealth, rising up at Makhzam.*

He means the camels of blood-money, and for this reason he said "rising up at Makhram" (in the text as: *ṭāli'āt bi-makhram*).

Among the people of the villages who make orchards, it dominates over palm trees. They say: "So-and-so went out to his wealth," meaning to his gardens. In the speech of Abu Hurayra: "Indeed my brothers the Ansar were preoccupied by work on their wealth." And Abu Talhah said: "Indeed the dearest of my wealth to me is Bi'ruha'."

Among the people of Makkah it dominated for dirhams, because the people of Makkah are people of trade. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to al-'Abbas: "Where is the wealth that is with Umm al-Fadl?"

It has preceded in His words, Most High: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:92], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The meaning of *'addadahu* is more than *'addahu*, that is: calculating it, because of the intensity of his passion for gathering it. Thus the doubling is for intensification of *'adda* and repeating it.

The majority read ﴿gathered wealth﴾ with the *mim* lightened. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, Ruways from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with the *mim* doubled, to match His words "counted it" (*'addadahu*), and it is an intensification of *jama'a*. On the reading of the majority, the doubling of *'addadahu* indicates the sense of striving to gather it, by way of *kinayah* (metonymy), because he does not repeat his counting except to increase his gathering.

It is also possible that *'addadahu* means: more than preparing it, that is, preparing its kinds, and it is then like His words, Most High: ﴿and the heaped-up hoards of gold and silver, and the branded horses, and the cattle and tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:14].

The clause ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *humazah*, and then it is used in mockery of him for his greed in gathering wealth and counting it, because there is no one who thinks that his wealth makes him immortal. So the statement falls under illustrative comparison (*tamthil*). Or the circumstantial clause may be intended for an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*).

[Page 539] It is also possible that the clause is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), and the predicate is used for denial, or with an omitted interrogative hamza, used in mockery of him, that he is certain his wealth will make him immortal, as if its immortalizing him had already happened and was established.

The *hamza* in *akhladahu* is for causation, that is: he made him immortal.

The majority read *yahsibu* with a kasra on the *sin*. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the *sin*, and both are dialects.

The meaning of the verse: those who gathered wealth are like one who thinks that wealth will protect them from death and make them immortal, because immortality in this world is their furthest wish, since they do not believe in another eternal life.

*Kalla* ("No!") is a negation of wealth making them immortal, and a deterrent from engaging in that shameful state which has placed them in the condition of one who thinks that wealth makes its owner immortal. Or it is a negation of greed in gathering wealth in a way that prevents them from giving God's rights in wealth, such as expenditures and zakat.

**[p. 540]**

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), arising from what the sentence ﴿he thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ [al-Humazah: 3] contains of mockery and denunciation, and from the meaning of threat that the particle of rebuke conveys.

The meaning is: he will surely be destroyed, so he will surely be thrown into the Crusher.

The *lam* is the answer to an implied oath, and the pronoun refers to *al-Humazah*.

**[p. 540 continued]**

Al-*nabdh* means to throw or cast down, and it is used mostly for throwing away what is disliked. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said, regarding the words of the Most High ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 40], that He likened them, in contempt of them, to pebbles that someone takes in his palm and then tosses away. End of quote.

Al-*Hutamah* is a descriptive noun on the pattern *fu'alah*, like what preceded in the case of *al-Humazah*. That is: he will be thrown into something that crushes it, i.e., breaks and grinds it.

The apparent reading is that the *lam* is for definiteness by prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), because he treated the descriptive term as a proper name by dominance, applied to something that crushes, and by it is meant Hell. The application of this term to Hell is one of the technical terms (*mustalahat*) of the Qur'an; in Arabic usage, this term is not applied to fire.

Surat al-Fil

Its name appeared in the speech of some of the early generations (salaf) as "Surat (Alam tara)" ("Have you not seen"). Al-Qurtubi related in his tafsir, in the commentary on Surat Quraysh, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "I prayed Maghrib behind 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he recited in the second rak'ah (Alam tara) and (li-ilafi Quraysh)." Likewise al-Bukhari titled it so. It was named Surat al-Fil in all the mushafs (copies of the Qur'an) and books of tafsir.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the nineteenth in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat (Qul ya ayyuha al-kafirun) and before Surat al-Falaq. It was also said to have been revealed before Surat Quraysh, based on al-Akhfash's view that His saying: ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ ("for the accustomedness of Quraysh," 106:1) is connected to His saying: ﴿فَجَعَلَهم كَعَصْفٍ مَأْكُولٍ﴾ ("and He made them like eaten straw," 105:5). Also, Ubayy ibn Ka'b made it and Surat Quraysh one surah in his mushaf, without separating them with the basmalah. And there is the report of 'Amr ibn Maymun from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab mentioned just above: it is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once recited in Maghrib, in the second rak'ah, Surat al-Fil and Surat Quraysh. That is, the Companions did not recite two surahs in one rak'ah of an obligatory prayer, since the sunnah is reciting al-Fatihah and one surah; this indicates that for him they were one surah. It is possible, however, that Surat Quraysh was revealed after Surat al-Falaq and was attached to Surat al-Fil, so the argument from Ubayy ibn Ka'b's mushaf and from what 'Amr ibn Maymun related is not conclusive.

Its verses are five.

* * *

It contains a reminder that the Ka'bah is the sanctuary of Allah, and that Allah protected it from those who intended harm against it, or made His anger manifest against them and punished them, because they did wrong by their greed to demolish the Mosque of Ibrahim, which they had in their own scripture. This is what Allah called a plot (kayd). It also serves so that what befell them would be a reminder to Quraysh that the doer of that is the Lord of that House, and that the idols they set up around it have no share in it.

Warning Quraysh, or reminding them, of the honor of the Prophet (ﷺ) with Allah, as He destroyed the People of the Elephant in the year of his birth (ﷺ).

Beyond this is the strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), that Allah repels from him the plot of the polytheists. For the One who repelled the plot of one who plotted against His House is more worthy to repel the plot of one who plots against His Messenger (ﷺ) and his religion. This is hinted at by His saying: ﴿ألَمْ نَجْعَلْ كَيْدَهم في تَضْلِيلٍ﴾ ("Did He not make their plot into confusion?", 105:2).

Beyond all of that is the reminder that Allah is dominant over His affair, and that the strength of the polytheists and the abundance of their numbers should not deceive them, nor should the gathering of their tribes against the Prophet (ﷺ) weaken him, for Allah destroyed those who were stronger than them in power and greater in number.

The mention of the destruction of the People of the Elephant is not repeated in the Qur'an, unlike the stories of other nations, for two reasons: first, the destruction of the People of the Elephant was not because of their denying a messenger from Allah; second, so that the polytheists would not take from it a pretext for pride in a standing they had with Allah, like their pride in their saying related in His saying: ﴿أجَعَلْتُمْ سِقايَةَ الحاجِّ وعِمارَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ كَمَن آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ ("Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of al-Masjid al-Haram equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day?", 9:19), and His saying: ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("And they bar access to al-Masjid al-Haram, though they were not its guardians. Its guardians are only the righteous, but most of them do not know.", 8:34).

It is counted as the nineteenth in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat (Qul ya ayyuha al-kafirun) and before Surat al-Falaq. It was also said to have been revealed before Surat Quraysh, based on al-Akhfash's view that His saying: ﴿لِإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ ("for the accustomedness of Quraysh," 106:1) is connected to His saying: ﴿فَجَعَلَهم كَعَصْفٍ مَأْكُولٍ﴾ ("and He made them like eaten straw," 105:5). Also, Ubayy ibn Ka'b made it and Surat Quraysh one surah in his mushaf, without separating them with the basmalah. And there is the report of 'Amr ibn Maymun from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab mentioned just above: it is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once recited in Maghrib, in the second rak'ah, Surat al-Fil and Surat Quraysh. That is, the Companions did not recite two surahs in one rak'ah of an obligatory prayer, since the sunnah is reciting al-Fatihah and one surah; this indicates that for him they were one surah. It is possible, however, that Surat Quraysh was revealed after Surat al-Falaq and was attached to Surat al-Fil, so the argument from Ubayy ibn Ka'b's mushaf and from what 'Amr ibn Maymun related is not conclusive.

Its verses are five.

* * *

It contains a reminder that the Ka'bah is the sanctuary of Allah, and that Allah protected it from those who intended harm against it, or made His anger manifest against them and punished them, because they did wrong by their greed to demolish the Mosque of Ibrahim, which they had in their own scripture. This is what Allah called a plot (kayd). It also serves so that what befell them would be a reminder to Quraysh that the doer of that is the Lord of that House, and that the idols they set up around it have no share in it.

Warning Quraysh, or reminding them, of the honor of the Prophet (ﷺ) with Allah, as He destroyed the People of the Elephant in the year of his birth (ﷺ).

Beyond this is the strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), that Allah repels from him the plot of the polytheists. For the One who repelled the plot of one who plotted against His House is more worthy to repel the plot of one who plots against His Messenger (ﷺ) and his religion. This is hinted at by His saying: ﴿ألَمْ نَجْعَلْ كَيْدَهم في تَضْلِيلٍ﴾ ("Did He not make their plot into confusion?", 105:2).

Beyond all of that is the reminder that Allah is dominant over His affair, and that the strength of the polytheists and the abundance of their numbers should not deceive them, nor should the gathering of their tribes against the Prophet (ﷺ) weaken him, for Allah destroyed those who were stronger than them in power and greater in number.

The mention of the destruction of the People of the Elephant is not repeated in the Qur'an, unlike the stories of other nations, for two reasons: first, the destruction of the People of the Elephant was not because of their denying a messenger from Allah; second, so that the polytheists would not take from it a pretext for pride in a standing they had with Allah, like their pride in their saying related in His saying: ﴿أجَعَلْتُمْ سِقايَةَ الحاجِّ وعِمارَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ كَمَن آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ ("Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of al-Masjid al-Haram equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day?", 9:19), and His saying: ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("And they bar access to al-Masjid al-Haram, though they were not its guardians. Its guardians are only the righteous, but most of them do not know.", 8:34).
